notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: State Ohm's law and the three equivalent expressions for electrical power.
notes.back:
V = I·R
P = V·I = I²·R = V²/R

Robotics use: sizing resistors, wire gauge, regulator heat, battery current.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Voltage divider: give the formula and one correct and one incorrect use on a robot.
notes.back:
Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2)

Correct: scaling a 5 V signal down to 3.3 V (R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ → 3.33 V); reading resistive sensors; battery-voltage monitoring on an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) pin.
Incorrect: as a power supply — output sags as soon as a load draws current.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: How do you size the series resistor for an LED? Work the example: 5 V supply, forward voltage 2 V, target 10 mA.
notes.back: R = (V<sub>supply</sub> − V<sub>forward</sub>) / I = (5 − 2) / 0.010 = 300 Ω → use the next standard value, 330 Ω.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What problem does a pull-up (or pull-down) resistor solve, and how does Arduino's INPUT_PULLUP change the button logic?
notes.back:
A disconnected (floating) input picks up noise and reads randomly. A pull-up (~10 kΩ to Vcc) or pull-down (to ground) defines the idle level.

pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP) enables the internal ~20–50 kΩ pull-up, so the button is wired pin → ground and reads LOW when pressed (active-low).
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: What is a decoupling (bypass) capacitor, and what is the standard practice for placing them?
notes.back:
A small capacitor between an Integrated Circuit's (IC) supply pin and ground that supplies fast transient current locally and shunts high-frequency noise.

Practice: 100 nF ceramic as close as possible to every IC supply pin, plus bulk electrolytic capacitance (100–1000 µF) near motor drivers and servo rails.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why does every relay, solenoid or brushed motor switched by a transistor need a flyback diode?
notes.back:
Inductor current cannot stop instantly: V = −L·di/dt produces a large voltage spike when the switch opens, which destroys the transistor.

A diode in reverse-parallel across the load gives the current a path to decay. (H-bridge driver ICs usually have these built in or use the MOSFET body diodes.)
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Describe the standard circuit for switching a high-current load from a microcontroller pin with an N-channel Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor (MOSFET).
notes.back:
Low-side switch: load between V+ and drain, source to ground, gate driven by the pin.
• Use a logic-level MOSFET (RDS(on) specified at 4.5 V or 2.5 V gate drive).
• ~100–220 Ω series gate resistor (limits the gate charging current).
• ~10 kΩ gate-to-source pull-down (keeps it off during reset).
• Flyback diode if the load is inductive.
• Common ground between load supply and microcontroller.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: You must connect a 5 V Arduino to a 3.3 V sensor or Raspberry Pi. What are the level-shifting options, and what is the risk if you skip them?
notes.back:
Risk: 5 V into a non-5 V-tolerant 3.3 V input forward-biases the protection diodes and can destroy the pin.

Options:
• Resistor divider — one direction, slow signals only.
• BSS138 MOSFET bidirectional shifter — ideal for Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C).
• Dedicated translator IC (e.g. 74LVC245, TXS0108).

3.3 V → 5 V input usually works without shifting but is marginal (ATmega328P needs ≥ 0.6·Vcc = 3.0 V for HIGH).
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Lithium-Polymer (LiPo) batteries: give cell voltages, what '3S 2200 mAh 25C' means, and the main safety rules.
notes.back:
Per cell: 3.7 V nominal, 4.2 V full, do not discharge below ~3.0–3.3 V.
3S = 3 cells in series = 11.1 V nominal (12.6 V full).
Max continuous current = capacity × C-rating = 2.2 Ah × 25 = 55 A.

Safety: balance-charge with a LiPo charger, use a low-voltage cutoff/alarm, never puncture or charge unattended — fire hazard.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Linear regulator vs. buck (step-down switching) converter: how do they differ and which do you use to power a Raspberry Pi from a 12 V robot battery?
notes.back:
Linear: burns the excess as heat, Ploss = (Vin − Vout)·I. Simple and low-noise, but 12 V → 5 V at 3 A would dissipate 21 W.
Buck: switches an inductor, ~85–95 % efficient, slightly noisier.

→ Use a buck converter rated for the Pi's peak current (Pi 5: 5 V / 5 A).
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Why must all boards on a robot share a common ground, and how do you keep motor currents from corrupting logic signals?
notes.back:
A signal voltage only has meaning relative to a shared 0 V reference; without it, levels are undefined and communication fails or damages pins.

Keep it clean: star-ground at the battery/regulator, route heavy motor return currents on their own thick wires (not through the logic ground), and decouple locally.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::01 Electronics Fundamentals
notes.front: Symptom: the microcontroller resets whenever the motors start. Cause and fixes?
notes.back:
Cause: motor inrush/stall current sags the supply rail below the brown-out threshold (or injects noise).

Fixes: separate regulator (or battery) for logic; bulk capacitor across the motor supply; never power servos/motors from the Arduino 5 V pin; thicker/shorter power wiring; ceramic capacitors across brushed motor terminals; keep common ground.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 01 Electronics Fundamentals

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Microcontroller Unit (MCU) vs. Microprocessor Unit (MPU): what is the difference and why do robots usually need both?
notes.back:
MCU: CPU + flash + RAM + peripherals (timers, ADC, PWM) on one chip; runs bare-metal or a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS); deterministic microsecond timing. Examples: ATmega328P, STM32, ESP32, RP2040.
MPU: CPU needing external RAM/storage; runs Linux; high throughput but non-deterministic timing. Examples: Raspberry Pi, Jetson.

Robots pair them: MPU for perception/planning, MCU for motor control and hard real-time I/O.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Arduino UNO R3: key specifications.
notes.back:
ATmega328P, 8-bit AVR @ 16 MHz
32 KB flash · 2 KB SRAM · 1 KB EEPROM
5 V logic
14 digital I/O (6 with Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM): 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11)
6 analog inputs, 10-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC)
External interrupts on pins 2 and 3
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Arduino UNO R4 (Minima / WiFi): what changed relative to the R3?
notes.back:
Renesas RA4M1, 32-bit Arm Cortex-M4 @ 48 MHz
256 KB flash · 32 KB SRAM
Still 5 V logic and the UNO form factor
14-bit ADC, a real 12-bit Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC), Controller Area Network (CAN) peripheral, USB-C
WiFi variant adds an ESP32-S3 radio module and a 12×8 LED matrix

Caveat: only ~8 mA per I/O pin (R3 tolerated 20 mA).
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Arduino UNO Q (2025): what is its 'dual-brain' architecture and why does it matter for robotics?
notes.back:
One board combining:
• Qualcomm Dragonwing QRB2210 Microprocessor Unit (MPU) — quad Arm Cortex-A53 @ 2.0 GHz, runs Debian Linux, 2 GB/16 GB or 4 GB/32 GB RAM/eMMC, Wi-Fi 5 + Bluetooth 5.1 → vision, AI inference, Python.
• STM32U585 Microcontroller Unit (MCU) — Arm Cortex-M33, runs Arduino sketches on Zephyr OS → deterministic real-time I/O.

A bridge library links the two; Arduino App Lab combines sketches, Python and AI models. It is the 'Linux computer + real-time MCU' robot pattern on a single UNO-sized board.
notes.source: Arduino UNO Q docs — https://docs.arduino.cc/hardware/uno-q · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: How do you convert an Arduino analogRead() value to volts, and what is the resolution on a 5 V UNO R3?
notes.back:
V = reading × Vref / 2n

UNO R3: 10-bit → 0…1023; 5 V / 1024 ≈ 4.88 mV per step.
More bits or a lower reference voltage (analogReference()) give finer resolution.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: What does analogWrite() actually output on an Arduino UNO R3?
notes.back:
Not an analog voltage — a Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) square wave: 8-bit duty cycle (0–255), ~490 Hz (≈980 Hz on pins 5 and 6).

Average voltage = duty × 5 V. Fine for LED dimming and motor-driver speed inputs; needs a low-pass filter to become a true analog level. (UNO R4 has a real DAC on A0.)
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Why is delay() a problem in robot code, and what is the standard non-blocking pattern?
notes.back:
delay() blocks the CPU: no sensor reads, no control updates, missed events.

Pattern ('blink without delay'):
unsigned long now = millis();
if (now - last >= interval) { last = now; task(); }

Each task gets its own timestamp, so many periodic jobs run cooperatively inside loop().
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: millis() overflows after about 49.7 days. How do you write timing code that survives the rollover?
notes.back:
Use unsigned long and always compare by subtraction:
if (millis() - start >= interval)

Unsigned modular arithmetic makes the difference correct across the wrap. Never write if (millis() >= start + interval) — the addition overflows.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: What are the rules for writing an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) on an Arduino?
notes.back:
• Keep it very short: set a flag or count, do the work in loop().
• No delay(), no Serial printing; millis() does not advance inside it.
• Shared variables must be volatile.
• On 8-bit AVR, multi-byte shared variables are not atomic — copy them inside noInterrupts() / interrupts().
• Attach with attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(pin), isr, RISING); on the UNO R3 only pins 2 and 3.

Typical use: wheel-encoder edges.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: What is switch bounce and how do you debounce in software?
notes.back:
Mechanical contacts chatter for ~1–20 ms, producing many edges per press.

Software debounce: accept a new state only after it has been stable for a debounce interval (e.g. 20–50 ms measured with millis()). Hardware alternative: RC filter + Schmitt trigger.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: On an Arduino UNO R3, which side effect does including the Servo library have?
notes.back:
The Servo library takes over Timer1, which disables analogWrite() Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) on pins 9 and 10.

General lesson: timers are shared hardware — libraries (Servo, tone, motor shields, encoder libraries) can conflict.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: How much current can an Arduino UNO R3 I/O pin supply, and what follows for driving motors or servos?
notes.back:
20 mA recommended (40 mA absolute maximum) per pin, ~200 mA total for the chip.

→ Never drive a motor, relay coil or servo power from an I/O pin or the 5 V pin. Use a transistor/MOSFET or a motor-driver IC with its own supply.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: ESP32: why is it popular in hobby robotics, and what are its pitfalls?
notes.back:
Dual-core 240 MHz (Xtensa LX6/LX7 or RISC-V variants), Wi-Fi + Bluetooth, many peripherals, FreeRTOS built in, programmable from the Arduino IDE, very cheap.

Pitfalls: 3.3 V logic (not 5 V tolerant); non-linear 12-bit Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC), and ADC2 is unusable while Wi-Fi is active; Wi-Fi current spikes (~500 mA) need a solid supply; some pins are boot-strapping pins.
notes.source: Espressif ESP32 docs — https://docs.espressif.com/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: Why structure robot firmware as a Finite State Machine (FSM)?
notes.back:
An FSM has explicit states (e.g. IDLE, SEARCH, APPROACH, GRAB, FAULT), transitions triggered by events/sensor conditions, and actions per state.

Benefits: non-blocking, predictable, easy to debug and extend, and gives you an obvious place for a safe FAULT state. Usually an enum + switch inside loop().
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: What does a Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) such as FreeRTOS or Zephyr give you over a bare-metal super-loop?
notes.back:
Pre-emptive, priority-based tasks with bounded latency, plus queues, semaphores/mutexes and software timers.

Use it when several activities with different rates and priorities must coexist (e.g. 1 kHz motor loop, 100 Hz sensor fusion, communications, logging). Costs: RAM per task stack, and new bug classes (priority inversion, races, deadlock).
notes.source: FreeRTOS docs — https://www.freertos.org/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::02 Microcontrollers & Arduino
notes.front: What is a watchdog timer and why should a mobile robot enable it?
notes.back:
A hardware countdown that resets the microcontroller unless the firmware periodically 'kicks' it. If code hangs (deadlock, stuck bus, runaway loop), the robot reboots into a safe state instead of driving on with stale motor commands.

Complement it with a command timeout: stop the motors if no fresh command arrives within e.g. 200 ms.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 02 Microcontrollers & Arduino

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Proprioceptive vs. exteroceptive sensors: define and give examples.
notes.back:
Proprioceptive — measure the robot's internal state: encoders, Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), motor current, joint torque, battery voltage.
Exteroceptive — measure the environment: camera, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), ultrasonic, tactile, Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS).
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: What does an Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) contain, and what do '6-axis' and '9-axis' mean?
notes.back:
• 3-axis accelerometer — specific force (gravity + linear acceleration).
• 3-axis gyroscope — angular velocity.
• (9-axis) 3-axis magnetometer — heading relative to Earth's field.

6-axis example: MPU-6050. 9-axis with on-chip fusion: BNO055. Roll and pitch are observable from gravity; yaw needs a magnetometer or another absolute reference.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Why fuse gyroscope and accelerometer data, and how does a complementary filter do it?
notes.back:
Gyro: smooth and fast, but integration drifts (bias). Accelerometer: drift-free gravity direction, but noisy and corrupted by motion.

Complementary filter:
θ = α·(θ + ω·dt) + (1 − α)·θaccel, α ≈ 0.95–0.98
= high-pass the gyro, low-pass the accelerometer. Cheap alternative to a Kalman filter; Madgwick/Mahony filters extend the idea to 3D with quaternions.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: How does an incremental quadrature encoder give both position and direction?
notes.back: Two channels, A and B, 90° out of phase. Which channel leads tells the direction; counting edges gives displacement. Counting all edges of both channels yields 4× the pulses per revolution. An optional index (Z) channel marks one absolute position per turn.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Incremental vs. absolute encoders: what is the practical difference for a robot arm?
notes.back:
Incremental: only counts change → position is lost at power-off → needs a homing routine.
Absolute (optical multi-track or magnetic, e.g. AS5600/AS5048): reports the true angle immediately at power-on → no homing; essential for arms and legged robots. Often placed on the joint output to see through gearbox backlash.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Compute the output-shaft resolution: 12 pulses-per-revolution encoder on the motor shaft, quadrature decoding, 50:1 gearbox.
notes.back:
Counts per output revolution = 12 × 4 × 50 = 2400
→ 360° / 2400 = 0.15° per count.

Distance per count for a wheel = π·D / 2400.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: How does an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor measure distance, and what are its limitations?
notes.back:
Send a 10 µs trigger → it emits a 40 kHz burst → echo pin stays HIGH for the round-trip time.
d = (t × 343 m/s) / 2 (speed of sound at ~20 °C). Range ≈ 2 cm – 4 m.

Limitations: wide cone (~15–30°), soft or angled surfaces reflect poorly, cross-talk between multiple sensors, slow update rate, temperature-dependent.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: How does Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) work and what types are used on robots?
notes.back:
Measures distance by laser time-of-flight (or phase shift / triangulation on cheap units).

• 2D spinning (e.g. RPLIDAR): one scan plane — the standard for indoor mapping and navigation.
• 3D multi-beam / solid-state: point clouds for outdoor robots and cars.
• Single-point Time-of-Flight (ToF) chips (e.g. VL53L1X): cheap short-range replacement for ultrasonic.

Weak on glass, mirrors and very dark surfaces.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Name the three depth-camera principles and their trade-offs.
notes.back:
• Passive/active stereo (e.g. Intel RealSense D4xx): triangulation between two cameras; works outdoors; struggles on texture-less surfaces unless an infrared projector adds texture.
• Structured light: project a known pattern; accurate at short range; fails in sunlight.
• Time-of-Flight (ToF): measure light round-trip per pixel; good at range; multipath and interference issues.

All output Red-Green-Blue-Depth (RGB-D) images → point clouds.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: What does a 6-axis force/torque sensor measure and where is it used?
notes.back:
Three forces (Fx, Fy, Fz) and three torques, usually via strain gauges, typically mounted at the wrist between arm and gripper.

Uses: contact detection, force-controlled assembly/insertion, polishing, hand-guiding (kinesthetic teaching), collision safety, and as an input modality for learned policies.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: What is a Hall-effect sensor and where does it appear in robots?
notes.back:
Outputs a voltage proportional to magnetic field (or a digital switch at a threshold).

Uses: rotor-position sensing for Brushless Direct-Current (BLDC) motor commutation, magnetic absolute encoders (AS5600), wheel-speed pickups, contact-less limit switches, and in-line current sensing.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: Distinguish accuracy, precision (repeatability) and resolution for a sensor.
notes.back:
Accuracy: closeness of the mean reading to the true value (systematic error/bias).
Precision: spread of repeated readings (random error).
Resolution: smallest change the sensor can report.

High resolution implies neither accuracy nor precision. Calibration fixes bias; filtering/averaging improves precision.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::03 Sensors
notes.front: What are vision-based tactile sensors (GelSight, DIGIT) and why do they matter for manipulation learning?
notes.back:
A camera looks at the back of a soft, illuminated elastomer 'skin'; contact deforms the gel, and the image encodes contact geometry, shear/slip and force at very high spatial resolution.

Because the output is an image, it plugs straight into vision encoders — several Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models add tactile tokens for contact-rich tasks such as insertion.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 03 Sensors

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Brushed Direct-Current (DC) motor: what sets its speed and its torque?
notes.back:
Speed ∝ applied voltage (minus back-EMF); torque ∝ current: τ = Kt·I.

Consequences: control speed with Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) duty cycle; measuring current gives a cheap torque estimate; stall = maximum current.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is an H-bridge, and why do hobbyists move from the L298N to MOSFET-based drivers?
notes.back:
Four switches around the motor; closing diagonal pairs reverses polarity → forward/reverse; Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) on the enable input sets speed; both low-side (or high-side) on = brake. Never close both switches on one side (shoot-through).

L298N uses bipolar transistors and drops ~2 V (hot, inefficient). MOSFET drivers (TB6612FNG, DRV8833, DRV8871) drop a fraction of a volt.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Hobby (RC) servo: what is the control signal and what is inside?
notes.back:
Signal: 50 Hz pulse train (20 ms period); pulse width 1.0–2.0 ms maps to roughly 0–180°, 1.5 ms = centre (many accept 0.5–2.5 ms).

Inside: DC motor + gearbox + potentiometer + a small closed-loop position controller. No position feedback to the user. Power from a separate 5–6 V rail; stall current can exceed 1 A.
notes.source: Arduino Documentation — https://docs.arduino.cc/ · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Stepper motors: how do they work, and what are the strengths and weaknesses?
notes.back:
Energising coils in sequence moves the rotor in fixed steps — typically 1.8° = 200 steps/rev; microstepping (e.g. 1/16 → 3200 steps/rev) smooths motion. Driver ICs (A4988, DRV8825, TMC2209) regulate coil current by chopping; control via STEP/DIR pins.

+ Precise open-loop positioning, holding torque.
− Torque falls with speed; lost steps go undetected without an encoder; draws full current at standstill; resonance.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Brushless Direct-Current (BLDC) motor vs. brushed motor.
notes.back:
No brushes: permanent-magnet rotor, three-phase stator, commutated electronically by a controller using Hall sensors, an encoder or sensorless back-EMF.

+ Higher efficiency and power density, long life, less electrical noise.
− Needs a three-phase inverter/controller (Electronic Speed Controller (ESC) or Field-Oriented Control drive).

Standard in drones, quadrupeds, humanoids and modern robot arms.
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is Field-Oriented Control (FOC)?
notes.back:
Vector control of a three-phase motor: measure phase currents → Clarke transform (3-phase → α/β) → Park transform using the rotor angle (→ rotating d/q frame). In that frame currents are DC quantities, so simple PI loops regulate Iq (torque-producing) and hold Id ≈ 0; inverse transforms + space-vector PWM drive the inverter.

Result: smooth, quiet, efficient torque control down to zero speed — the basis of torque-controlled robot joints (ODrive, SimpleFOC, moteus).
notes.source: SimpleFOC docs — https://docs.simplefoc.com/ · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: A gearbox has ratio N:1. How do speed, torque and reflected rotor inertia change at the output?
notes.back:
Speed ÷ N · Torque × N (× efficiency) · Reflected rotor inertia × N²

High ratios give torque but make the joint slow, hard to back-drive, and hide external forces behind friction and reflected inertia.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: On a DC motor's torque–speed line, where is mechanical power maximal?
notes.back:
Torque falls linearly from stall torque (zero speed) to zero at no-load speed.
P = τ·ω is maximal at half the no-load speed and half the stall torque.

Choose motor + gear ratio so the operating point sits near this region, not near stall (overheating).
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is back-electromotive force (back-EMF)?
notes.back:
A spinning motor acts as a generator: Vemf = Ke·ω, opposing the applied voltage. Current is I = (V − Keω)/R, so current (and torque) are highest at stall and drop as speed rises.

Uses: sensorless speed estimation/commutation. Hazard: an externally driven or braking motor pumps energy back into the supply (regeneration).
notes.source: Hughes & Drury, Electric Motors and Drives (5th ed.) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a Quasi-Direct-Drive (QDD) or 'proprioceptive' actuator, and why did it transform legged robots?
notes.back:
A high-torque-density 'pancake' Brushless DC motor with a low gear ratio (roughly 6:1–10:1) and no torque sensor.

Low reflected inertia and friction make it back-drivable and impact-tolerant, and joint torque can be controlled accurately from motor current alone. Pioneered in the MIT Cheetah; now standard in quadrupeds (Unitree) and many humanoids — and well suited to policies trained with reinforcement learning because it is easy to simulate.
notes.source: Wensing et al. 2017, Proprioceptive Actuator Design in the MIT Cheetah (IEEE T-RO) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a Series Elastic Actuator (SEA)?
notes.back:
A deliberately compliant spring between gearbox and load. Measuring spring deflection gives joint torque (Hooke's law), turning force control into a position-control problem.

+ Accurate force control, shock tolerance, energy storage.
− Lower control bandwidth.
Used in Baxter, NASA Valkyrie, ANYmal (ANYdrive).
notes.source: Pratt & Williamson 1995, Series Elastic Actuators (IROS) · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: Compare the three reducer types common in robot joints: planetary, strain-wave (harmonic) and cycloidal.
notes.back:
Planetary: cheap, efficient, back-drivable at low ratios; has backlash. Used in Quasi-Direct-Drive (QDD) legs.
Strain-wave (Harmonic Drive): ~50–160:1 in one compact stage, near-zero backlash; costly, some compliance, poor back-drivability. The classic industrial/collaborative arm joint.
Cycloidal: high ratio, very robust to shock loads, low backlash; heavier, some vibration.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::04 Actuators & Power Transmission
notes.front: What is a 'smart' bus servo (Dynamixel, Feetech STS3215) and why do low-cost learning arms such as the SO-101 use them?
notes.back:
A servo with its own microcontroller on a daisy-chained serial bus (half-duplex TTL or RS-485). Each unit has an ID and reports position, velocity, load, voltage and temperature; supports position/velocity/current modes and torque-off.

For imitation learning this gives readable joint states on both the hand-moved leader arm and the follower arm with minimal wiring — the basis of the SO-100/SO-101 used with Hugging Face LeRobot.
notes.source: Hugging Face LeRobot — https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot · SmolVLA https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01844 · 04 Actuators & Power Transmission

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter (UART): how does it work and what does '115200 8N1' mean?
notes.back:
Asynchronous point-to-point serial: TX → RX crossed, plus common ground; no clock line, so both ends must agree on the baud rate.

115200 8N1 = 115 200 bit/s, 8 data bits, No parity, 1 stop bit (each byte framed by a start bit and a stop bit → 10 bits on the wire per byte).
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Inter-Integrated Circuit (I2C): wiring, addressing, speeds, and the classic failure modes.
notes.back:
Two open-drain lines — SDA (data) and SCL (clock) — with pull-up resistors (~2.2–10 kΩ); one controller, many targets selected by 7-bit address. 100 kbit/s standard, 400 kbit/s fast, 1 Mbit/s fast-mode plus.

Failure modes: missing pull-ups; two devices with the same fixed address (fix: address pins or a TCA9548A multiplexer); long wires (bus capacitance); a target holding SDA low after a glitch (bus lock-up).
notes.source: NXP UM10204 I2C-bus specification · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI): wiring and characteristics.
notes.back:
Four wires: SCK (clock), MOSI/COPI, MISO/CIPO, and one Chip Select (CS) line per device. Full-duplex, push-pull, no addressing, tens of Mbit/s.

Must match clock polarity/phase (mode 0–3). Used for fast devices: displays, SD cards, high-rate IMUs, external ADCs, encoder chips.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: UART vs. I2C vs. SPI — how do you choose?
notes.back:
UART: two devices, simple streams (GPS, Bluetooth module, board-to-board link).
I2C: many slow sensors on two wires, short distances.
SPI: high data rate or low latency, few devices, more wires.

None of the three is robust over long, noisy cables — use differential buses (CAN, RS-485) for that.
notes.source: SparkFun Learn tutorials — https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Controller Area Network (CAN) bus: how does it work?
notes.back:
Two-wire differential bus (CAN_H / CAN_L), multi-master, 120 Ω termination at each end. Messages carry an identifier, not an address; every node sees every frame. Non-destructive bitwise arbitration: dominant 0 beats recessive 1, so the lowest ID wins = highest priority. Built-in CRC, acknowledgement and automatic retransmission.

Classical CAN: ≤ 1 Mbit/s, 8 data bytes.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation — https://www.can-cia.org/ · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What does CAN FD add, and why is CAN the default bus for robot joint actuators?
notes.back:
CAN with Flexible Data-rate (CAN FD): up to 64 data bytes per frame and a faster data phase (typically 2–8 Mbit/s).

Why CAN in robots: noise immunity near motors, only two wires daisy-chained through the limbs, deterministic priority, built-in error handling, cheap transceivers — used by ODrive, moteus, MIT Mini Cheetah-style actuators and many humanoids.
notes.source: Bosch CAN 2.0 spec / CAN in Automation — https://www.can-cia.org/ · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What is RS-485 and where is it used in robotics?
notes.back:
A differential electrical standard (not a protocol): multi-drop (32+ nodes), long cables (up to ~1200 m at low rates), usually half-duplex with a driver-enable line; needs termination and biasing.

Carries Modbus RTU, Dynamixel Protocol 2.0, DMX and many industrial sensor links. Unlike CAN it has no arbitration or error handling — the protocol on top must provide them.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What is EtherCAT and why do high-performance arms and humanoids use it?
notes.back:
Ethernet for Control Automation Technology: a master sends one Ethernet frame through all devices in a line/ring; each device reads and writes its data on the fly in hardware as the frame passes. Distributed clocks synchronise nodes to well under a microsecond.

→ Cycle times of 1 ms down to ~100 µs with dozens of axes; standard Ethernet hardware on the master side.
notes.source: EtherCAT Technology Group — https://www.ethercat.org/ · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: Why should you never close a fast control loop over Wi-Fi, and how is wireless used properly on robots?
notes.back:
Wi-Fi/Bluetooth latency is variable (milliseconds to seconds) with packet loss and no determinism → instability if it sits inside a feedback loop.

Pattern: run stabilising loops on board; send only set-points, tele-operation commands and telemetry over wireless; add a command timeout/fail-safe; prefer UDP-style best-effort for fresh-data streams.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: When you design your own serial protocol between a Raspberry Pi and a microcontroller, what must every packet have?
notes.back:
• Framing: start byte/length, or Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing (COBS) with a 0x00 delimiter, so the receiver can resynchronise mid-stream.
• Integrity: checksum or Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC).
• Message ID/type and fixed binary layout (mind endianness and struct padding).
• Timeouts and sequence numbers for lost packets.

Or use an existing solution: micro-ROS, MAVLink, Protocol Buffers/nanopb.
notes.source: Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics (3rd ed.) · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::05 Communication Protocols
notes.front: What is MAVLink?
notes.back: Micro Air Vehicle Link: a lightweight binary messaging protocol between drones/rovers, companion computers and ground stations. Defines messages such as HEARTBEAT, ATTITUDE, GLOBAL_POSITION_INT and commands/missions; MAVLink 2 adds signing. Used by PX4 and ArduPilot with QGroundControl; bridges to ROS 2 exist (MAVROS; PX4 also offers a native uXRCE-DDS bridge).
notes.source: MAVLink developer guide — https://mavlink.io/ · 05 Communication Protocols

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why is a Raspberry Pi not a drop-in replacement for an Arduino in a robot?
notes.back:
A Pi is a Linux Single-Board Computer (SBC): powerful, networked, runs Python/OpenCV/ROS 2 — but it has non-deterministic timing (scheduler jitter), no analog inputs, fragile 3.3 V I/O, slow boot, and needs a clean shutdown.

An Arduino-class microcontroller gives microsecond-deterministic I/O, ADC, hardware timers and instant boot. → Use both.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Raspberry Pi 5: key specifications relevant to robotics.
notes.back:
Broadcom BCM2712: 4× Arm Cortex-A76 @ 2.4 GHz (≈2–3× Pi 4), VideoCore VII GPU; up to 16 GB RAM.
RP1 in-house I/O controller (GPIO, USB, Ethernet, camera ports hang off it via PCIe).
PCIe 2.0 ×1 connector → NVMe storage or AI accelerators.
2× 4-lane camera/display (MIPI) ports, real-time clock, power button.
Needs 5 V / 5 A USB-C supply; active cooling recommended.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What are the electrical rules for the Raspberry Pi 40-pin General-Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) header?
notes.back:
• 3.3 V logic, NOT 5 V tolerant — a 5 V signal can kill the pin/SoC.
• ~16 mA max per pin, ~50 mA total across pins — drive loads through transistors/drivers.
• No analog inputs — add an external ADC (MCP3008 on SPI, ADS1115 on I2C).
• Header also exposes I2C, SPI, UART and two hardware PWM channels, plus 5 V and 3.3 V rails.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: GPIO code that worked on a Raspberry Pi 4 fails on a Pi 5. Why, and what should you use?
notes.back:
On the Pi 5 the GPIO lives on the separate RP1 chip, so libraries that poke the SoC's registers directly (classic RPi.GPIO, pigpio) no longer work.

Use the kernel's character-device interface: libgpiod, lgpio/rpi-lgpio, or gpiozero (which selects a working backend).
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Why does software Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) from Linux make servos jitter, and what are the fixes?
notes.back:
User-space timing is pre-empted by the scheduler, so pulse widths wobble by tens to hundreds of microseconds.

Fixes: the Pi's hardware PWM channels; a dedicated I2C PWM chip — PCA9685 (16 channels, 12-bit); or hand servo/motor timing to a microcontroller.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is PREEMPT_RT and what does it not give you?
notes.back:
The real-time pre-emption patch set for Linux, merged into the mainline kernel in version 6.12 (2024). It makes almost all kernel code pre-emptible and turns interrupt handlers into schedulable threads → bounded worst-case latency (tens to ~100 µs) for high-priority SCHED_FIFO threads.

It does not make code faster, and you must still avoid page faults (mlockall), dynamic allocation and blocking I/O in the real-time path. Enough for ~1 kHz loops (ros2_control, EtherCAT masters).
notes.source: Linux kernel real-time docs — https://wiki.linuxfoundation.org/realtime/start · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Describe the canonical two-tier compute architecture of a hobby-to-research mobile robot.
notes.back:
High level — Linux computer (Raspberry Pi / Jetson): cameras, LiDAR, SLAM, planning, ROS 2, networking, AI inference.
Low level — microcontroller: encoder counting, PID motor loops at 100 Hz–1 kHz+, IMU reads, safety timeouts.

Link: USB/UART, CAN or micro-ROS. Interface contract: velocity commands down (e.g. cmd_vel), odometry + sensor data up.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How do you use cameras on a current Raspberry Pi?
notes.back:
Camera modules connect over the MIPI Camera Serial Interface (CSI-2) ribbon. The software stack is libcamera: command-line rpicam-apps (rpicam-hello, rpicam-still, rpicam-vid) and the Picamera2 Python library.

The legacy stack (raspistill, original picamera) is gone. USB webcams still appear as V4L2 devices for OpenCV's VideoCapture.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: What is the Raspberry Pi AI HAT+?
notes.back:
A Hardware Attached on Top (HAT+) board for the Pi 5 with a Hailo neural accelerator on the PCIe link: Hailo-8L, 13 Tera-Operations Per Second (TOPS) or Hailo-8, 26 TOPS. Integrated with the camera stack (rpicam-apps) for real-time object detection, segmentation and pose estimation at a few watts.

It accelerates compiled vision networks — it is not a CUDA GPU and does not run large vision-language-action models.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: When do you step up from a Raspberry Pi to an NVIDIA Jetson?
notes.back:
When you need an on-board CUDA GPU: deep-learning perception, GPU-accelerated SLAM (Isaac ROS), or running learned policies.

• Jetson Orin Nano Super — up to 67 TOPS, entry level.
• Jetson AGX Orin — up to 275 TOPS.
• Jetson AGX Thor (2025) — Blackwell GPU, up to 2070 FP4 teraFLOPS, 128 GB memory; aimed at humanoids running foundation models on board.
notes.source: NVIDIA Jetson — https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded-computing · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Two reliability killers on Pi-based robots are power and storage. Symptoms and countermeasures?
notes.back:
Under-voltage: throttling, random reboots, USB drop-outs when motors start. Check with vcgencmd get_throttled (non-zero = trouble). Use a dedicated 5 V / 5 A buck converter and short, thick leads.

SD-card corruption after hard power cuts: provide a clean-shutdown path, use a read-only/overlay root filesystem, or boot from NVMe/SSD; log to RAM or external storage.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Outline a minimal OpenCV colour-tracking pipeline that steers a robot toward a coloured ball.
notes.back:
1. Grab frame (Picamera2 or VideoCapture).
2. Convert BGR → Hue-Saturation-Value (HSV) — hue is robust to lighting.
3. inRange() threshold → binary mask; clean with erode/dilate.
4. findContours() → largest contour → centroid (image moments) and area.
5. Error = centroid x − image centre → steering controller; area → distance proxy.

Send the command to the motor microcontroller; keep resolution low for frame rate.
notes.source: OpenCV docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: Raspberry Pi Pico vs. Raspberry Pi: what is the Pico, and what is special about its chips?
notes.back:
The Pico is a microcontroller board, not a Linux computer.
• RP2040: dual Arm Cortex-M0+ @ 133 MHz, 264 KB SRAM.
• RP2350 (Pico 2): dual Cortex-M33 or dual Hazard3 RISC-V @ 150 MHz, 520 KB SRAM, security features.

Special: Programmable I/O (PIO) state machines that implement custom, cycle-exact protocols in hardware (quadrature decoding, WS2812 LEDs, extra UARTs). Program with C/C++ SDK, MicroPython or Arduino core.
notes.source: Raspberry Pi Documentation — https://www.raspberrypi.com/documentation/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux
notes.front: How do you run the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) on a Raspberry Pi?
notes.back:
ROS 2 binary packages target Ubuntu (Tier 1, arm64) → simplest: install 64-bit Ubuntu on the Pi and apt install the matching distribution.

On Raspberry Pi OS (Debian-based): run ROS 2 in a Docker container or build from source.

Tip: keep heavy visualisation (RViz) on a laptop in the same network/ROS domain; run only drivers and navigation on the Pi.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 06 Raspberry Pi & Embedded Linux

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Open-loop vs. closed-loop control.
notes.back:
Open-loop: command computed without measuring the result (stepper moves, timed driving). Simple, but blind to disturbances and model error.
Closed-loop (feedback): measure output, compute error e = r − y, correct continuously. Rejects disturbances and tolerates model error — at the risk of instability if badly tuned.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Write the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control law and state what each term does.
notes.back:
u(t) = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt + Kd·de/dt

P — reacts to present error; more gain = faster but more overshoot.
I — accumulates past error; removes steady-state error; adds phase lag/overshoot.
D — reacts to the error's rate; adds damping; amplifies noise.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: A proportional-only velocity loop on a wheel motor never quite reaches the set-point. Why, and what fixes it?
notes.back:
With P-only control, output requires error: holding speed against friction/load needs a non-zero command, hence a non-zero steady-state error (smaller with higher Kp, never zero).

Fix: add integral action, and/or a feedforward term that supplies the expected command directly.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What practical modifications make the derivative term of a PID controller usable on real hardware?
notes.back:
• Low-pass filter the derivative — raw differentiation amplifies sensor noise.
• Derivative on measurement (−Kd·dy/dt) instead of on error — avoids the 'derivative kick' when the set-point steps.
• Use a consistent, accurately known sample time dt.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is integral windup and how do you prevent it?
notes.back:
While the actuator is saturated (e.g. PWM at 100 %), the integrator keeps accumulating error it cannot act on; when the error finally reverses, the stored integral causes large overshoot and slow recovery.

Anti-windup: clamp the integrator; stop integrating while saturated (conditional integration); or back-calculation (bleed the integrator by the saturation excess).
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What does a discrete PID implementation on a microcontroller require that the textbook formula hides?
notes.back:
A fixed, known sample period: run the loop from a timer interrupt or a micros()-scheduled task; integral ≈ Σ e·dt, derivative ≈ Δ/dt.

Also: output clamping + anti-windup, derivative filtering, consistent units, and no blocking calls (Serial prints, delay) inside the loop. Timing jitter acts like noise on the D term.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain tuning: procedure and the classic PID settings.
notes.back:
1. Set Ki = Kd = 0.
2. Raise Kp until sustained oscillation: that gain is Ku, the period is Tu.
3. Classic PID: Kp = 0.6·Ku, Ti = Tu/2, Td = Tu/8 (→ Ki = 1.2·Ku/Tu, Kd = 0.075·Ku·Tu).

Gives an aggressive (~quarter-decay) response — a starting point, not a final tune. Do not drive fragile mechanisms to oscillation.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Name the four standard step-response performance metrics.
notes.back:
• Rise time — 10 % → 90 % of the final value.
• Overshoot — peak excess over the final value, in %.
• Settling time — time to stay within ±2 % (or 5 %).
• Steady-state error — remaining offset.

For a second-order system, overshoot is set by the damping ratio ζ and speed by the natural frequency ωn.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is cascaded control in a servo drive?
notes.back:
Nested loops: position loop → commands velocity → velocity loop → commands current/torque → current loop → drives the PWM voltage.

Each inner loop must be roughly 5–10× faster than the one around it (e.g. current 10–20 kHz, velocity ~1–5 kHz, position ~1 kHz). Benefits: disturbances are rejected close to where they enter; limits (current, speed) are enforced naturally; loops are tuned inside-out.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is feedforward control and why combine it with feedback?
notes.back:
Feedforward computes the command expected to be needed from a model and the reference (e.g. velocity × kv, acceleration × ka, gravity torque g(q)) and adds it to the feedback output.

It acts before error appears and does not affect stability; feedback then only handles model error and disturbances → better tracking with lower gains. Gravity compensation on an arm is the classic example.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: How fast must a digital control loop sample?
notes.back:
Shannon–Nyquist demands > 2× the highest signal frequency just to avoid aliasing, but for control the rule of thumb is 10–20× the desired closed-loop bandwidth (and an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC).

Delay matters as much as rate: computation + communication latency eats phase margin.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Write the linear state-space model and the stability condition in continuous and discrete time.
notes.back:
ẋ = A·x + B·u, y = C·x + D·u

Stable ⇔ all eigenvalues of A (the poles) have negative real part (left half-plane).
Discrete xk+1 = Adxk + Bduk: all eigenvalues inside the unit circle.

Non-linear robots are linearised around an operating point (e.g. the upright pendulum).
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Define controllability and observability and give the rank tests.
notes.back:
Controllable: inputs can drive the state anywhere in finite time ⇔ rank [B AB A²B … An−1B] = n.
Observable: the state can be reconstructed from outputs ⇔ rank [C; CA; …; CAn−1] = n.

Controllability permits arbitrary pole placement by state feedback; observability permits an observer/Kalman filter. Example: yaw is unobservable from an accelerometer alone.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is the Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR)?
notes.back:
Optimal state feedback u = −K·x minimising J = ∫ (xᵀQx + uᵀRu) dt for a linear system. K = R⁻¹BᵀP, where P solves the algebraic Riccati equation.

Tuning means choosing weights: Q penalises state error, R penalises actuator effort. Guaranteed stable with good margins (given full state). Workhorse for balancing robots, quadrotors and stabilising trajectories (time-varying LQR).
notes.source: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT 6.832) — https://underactuated.mit.edu/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is Model Predictive Control (MPC)?
notes.back:
At every step: solve a finite-horizon optimal-control problem from the current state using a model, subject to constraints (torque limits, friction cones, obstacles); apply only the first input; shift the horizon and repeat (receding horizon).

+ Handles constraints and preview explicitly.
− Needs a model and real-time optimisation.
Used for legged locomotion (MIT Cheetah convex MPC), autonomous driving, drones.
notes.source: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT 6.832) — https://underactuated.mit.edu/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What are gain margin and phase margin?
notes.back:
Robustness measures read from the open-loop frequency response:
Gain margin — factor by which loop gain can rise before instability (measured where phase = −180°).
Phase margin — extra phase lag tolerated (measured where gain = 1).

Typical targets: ≥ 6 dB and 45–60°. Time delay subtracts phase (−ω·Td) — why latency destabilises loops.
notes.source: Åström & Murray, Feedback Systems (2nd ed.) — https://fbswiki.org/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: Impedance control vs. admittance control.
notes.back:
Both regulate the dynamic relationship between motion and contact force instead of pure position or pure force — the robot behaves like a virtual mass-spring-damper: F = K(xd − x) + D(ẋd − ẋ).

Impedance: measure motion → command force/torque; needs torque-controllable, back-drivable joints.
Admittance: measure force → command motion; suits stiff, position-controlled industrial arms with a wrist force/torque sensor.

Essential for contact-rich manipulation and safe human interaction.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is computed-torque (inverse-dynamics) control of a manipulator?
notes.back:
τ = M(q)·(q̈d + Kdė + Kpe) + C(q,q̇)q̇ + g(q)

The model cancels the arm's non-linear, coupled dynamics (feedback linearisation), leaving decoupled linear error dynamics ë + Kdė + Kpe = 0 for each joint. Needs a good dynamic model and torque-controlled joints; more accurate at speed than independent joint PID.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::07 Control Theory
notes.front: What is Whole-Body Control (WBC) on a humanoid or legged robot?
notes.back:
A ~1 kHz controller that computes all joint torques at once by solving a constrained optimisation — usually a Quadratic Program (QP) — over the full floating-base dynamics.

Tasks (centre-of-mass/balance, foot and hand poses, posture) are weighted or strictly prioritised; constraints include contact friction cones, torque and joint limits. Typically sits beneath an MPC or footstep planner. Increasingly replaced or complemented by reinforcement-learned whole-body policies.
notes.source: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT 6.832) — https://underactuated.mit.edu/ · 07 Control Theory

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Define Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and state Grübler's formula.
notes.back:
DoF = the minimum number of independent coordinates that specify the configuration. A free rigid body has 6 in space, 3 in the plane.

Grübler: dof = m·(N − 1 − J) + Σ fi
m = 6 (spatial) or 3 (planar), N = links including ground, J = joints, fi = freedoms of joint i. (Valid when joint constraints are independent.)
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Configuration space (C-space), task space and workspace: distinguish them.
notes.back:
C-space: the space of all configurations q (e.g. joint angles); its dimension = DoF.
Task space: the space in which the task is expressed (e.g. end-effector pose in SE(3)).
Workspace: the set of poses/positions the end-effector can reach — a property of the robot, independent of the task.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What properties define a rotation matrix?
notes.back:
R ∈ SO(3): 3×3, RᵀR = I (orthonormal columns), det R = +1.

Hence R⁻¹ = Rᵀ; columns are the body-frame axes expressed in the reference frame; composition is matrix multiplication and does not commute. 9 numbers with 6 constraints → 3 DoF.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is gimbal lock?
notes.back:
A singularity of any three-angle (Euler / roll-pitch-yaw) parameterisation: at a particular middle angle (pitch = ±90° for roll-pitch-yaw) the first and third rotation axes align, one degree of freedom is lost and the angle rates blow up.

It is a defect of the representation, not of the physical rotation. Avoid by using rotation matrices or quaternions internally.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Why are unit quaternions the standard orientation representation in robot software?
notes.back:
q = (w, x, y, z), ‖q‖ = 1; encodes axis-angle as (cos θ/2, sin θ/2 · axis).

+ 4 numbers, no gimbal lock, cheap to compose and re-normalise, smooth interpolation via Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP).
− Double cover: q and −q are the same rotation (handle in filters and when averaging); not intuitive.

Beware conventions: ROS orders (x, y, z, w); Eigen's constructor takes (w, x, y, z).
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is a homogeneous transformation matrix?
notes.back:
T = [[R, p], [0 0 0, 1]] ∈ SE(3): a 4×4 matrix packing rotation R and translation p.

• Maps points between frames: pa = Tab·pb
• Chains by multiplication: Tac = Tab·Tbc
• Inverse: [[Rᵀ, −Rᵀp], [0, 1]]

The backbone of forward kinematics, camera extrinsics and ROS tf2.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Forward kinematics of a serial arm: definition and the two standard formulations.
notes.back:
Map joint values q to the end-effector pose T(q).

1. Denavit–Hartenberg (DH): attach a frame to each link by convention; multiply link transforms T = A1(q1)…An(qn).
2. Product of Exponentials (PoE): T(θ) = e[S1]θ1 … e[Sn]θn · M, with joint screw axes Si in the base frame and home pose M — no per-link frames needed.

Always unique and easy for serial chains (the opposite holds for parallel robots).
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What are the four Denavit–Hartenberg (DH) parameters?
notes.back:
Per joint/link:
• a — link length (distance along the common normal, x-axis)
• α — link twist (angle about x)
• d — link offset (distance along z, the joint axis)
• θ — joint angle (about z)

Revolute joint: θ is the variable; prismatic: d. Beware: 'standard' and 'modified' (Craig) conventions differ.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Inverse kinematics (IK): what makes it hard and how is it solved?
notes.back:
Find q such that T(q) = Tdesired. Non-linear; may have zero, several (e.g. up to 8 for a typical 6R arm with a spherical wrist) or infinitely many solutions.

• Analytic: closed form for special geometries (spherical wrist — Pieper); fast, all solutions.
• Numerical: Newton–Raphson, Δq = J⁺·e iterated from an initial guess; general, finds one nearby solution, may fail near singularities or joint limits. Optimisation-based solvers (TRAC-IK etc.) add limits and costs.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the manipulator Jacobian?
notes.back:
The configuration-dependent matrix mapping joint velocities to end-effector twist:
v = J(q)·q̇ (6×n for a spatial arm).

Used for velocity (resolved-rate) control, numerical IK, singularity and manipulability analysis, and force mapping. 'Geometric/space/body' Jacobians differ in the frame and representation of the twist.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is a kinematic singularity, what happens near one, and what is the standard numerical remedy?
notes.back:
A configuration where J(q) loses rank: the end-effector cannot move (or resist force) in some direction — e.g. arm fully stretched, or two wrist axes aligned.

Near it, the inverse demands huge joint velocities for small Cartesian motions.

Remedy: damped least squares, q̇ = Jᵀ(JJᵀ + λ²I)⁻¹·v — trades a little tracking error for bounded joint speeds; plus planning that avoids such regions (manipulability measure w = √det(JJᵀ)).
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: State the static force relationship between end-effector wrench and joint torques.
notes.back:
τ = Jᵀ(q)·F

(Follows from conservation of power: τᵀq̇ = Fᵀv.) Uses: gravity/payload torque estimation, implementing Cartesian impedance control with joint torques, estimating contact forces from motor currents. Near singularities small joint torques can resist very large forces in the singular direction.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is kinematic redundancy and how is the null space used?
notes.back:
More joints than task dimensions (e.g. 7-DoF arm for a 6-DoF pose) → infinitely many joint motions for one end-effector motion.

q̇ = J⁺·v + (I − J⁺J)·q̇0

The second term moves the joints without moving the end-effector — used for secondary objectives: avoiding joint limits, obstacles and singularities, or keeping an elbow posture.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Write the manipulator equation of motion and name each term.
notes.back:
M(q)·q̈ + C(q,q̇)·q̇ + g(q) = τ + Jᵀ(q)·Fext

M — symmetric positive-definite mass (inertia) matrix
C·q̇ — Coriolis and centrifugal terms
g — gravity torques
τ — joint torques; JᵀFext — external contact forces

Inverse dynamics (motion → torque; recursive Newton–Euler, O(n)) is used for control; forward dynamics (torque → acceleration) for simulation.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Differential-drive robot: give the forward kinematics.
notes.back:
With wheel linear speeds vr, vl (= radius × wheel angular speed) and track width L:
v = (vr + vl)/2, ω = (vr − vl)/L
ẋ = v·cos θ, ẏ = v·sin θ, θ̇ = ω

Inverse: vr,l = v ± ω·L/2 — exactly what a base controller does with a cmd_vel (v, ω) command.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is wheel odometry (dead reckoning) and why does it drift?
notes.back:
Integrating encoder-measured wheel motion through the kinematic model to estimate the pose.

Errors are integrated, so they grow without bound: wheel slip, uneven floors, unequal wheel diameters and uncertain track width (systematic → calibrate, e.g. UMBmark square test), finite encoder resolution. Heading error dominates because it converts into position error with distance travelled. → Fuse with an IMU and correct with exteroceptive localisation.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: Holonomic vs. non-holonomic mobile robots.
notes.back:
A non-holonomic constraint restricts velocities without reducing the reachable configurations: a differential-drive or car-like robot cannot slide sideways (ẏcos θ − ẋsin θ = 0) yet can reach any pose by manoeuvring (parallel parking).

Holonomic (omnidirectional) bases — mecanum or omni wheels — can command vx, vy and ω independently. Trade-off: rollers reduce traction, efficiency and odometry accuracy.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is an underactuated system? Give robotic examples.
notes.back:
A system with fewer independent actuators than degrees of freedom — it cannot command arbitrary instantaneous accelerations, so control must exploit the natural dynamics.

Examples: cart-pole, Acrobot, quadrotor (4 inputs, 6 DoF), and every legged robot (the floating base is unactuated; it is moved only through contact forces).
notes.source: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT 6.832) — https://underactuated.mit.edu/ · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the Zero Moment Point (ZMP) and how was it used for bipedal walking?
notes.back:
The point on the ground where the net horizontal moment of the contact forces is zero (equivalently the centre of pressure on flat ground). If the ZMP stays strictly inside the support polygon, the foot does not tip.

Classical humanoids (e.g. ASIMO) planned centre-of-mass trajectories with the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM) so that the ZMP tracks the footsteps — stable but flat-footed and conservative. Modern robots use MPC/whole-body control or reinforcement learning with dynamic contacts.
notes.source: Siciliano, Sciavicco, Villani & Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::08 Kinematics & Dynamics
notes.front: What is the 'floating base' model of a legged or humanoid robot?
notes.back:
The robot's state is the 6-DoF pose of a base link (unactuated) plus the n joint angles: q ∈ SE(3) × ℝⁿ. The equation of motion gains contact terms:
M(q)v̇ + h(q,v) = Sᵀτ + Σ Jcᵀ·fc
where S selects the actuated joints and fc are contact forces constrained to friction cones.

Locomotion = choosing contacts and contact forces to move the base.
notes.source: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT 6.832) — https://underactuated.mit.edu/ · 08 Kinematics & Dynamics

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Pinhole camera model: write the projection and name the intrinsic parameters.
notes.back:
u = fx·X/Z + cx, v = fy·Y/Z + cy

Intrinsic matrix K = [[fx, 0, cx], [0, fy, cy], [0, 0, 1]] — focal lengths in pixels and principal point. Full model: x ~ K·[R | t]·X, with extrinsics [R | t] giving the camera pose. Depth Z is lost in the projection.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What does camera calibration estimate and how is it done in practice?
notes.back:
Intrinsics (fx, fy, cx, cy) and lens distortion coefficients (radial k1,k2,k3; tangential p1,p2), optionally extrinsics.

Practice (Zhang's method): 15–30 images of a checkerboard/ChArUco board at varied poses → cv2.calibrateCamera → check reprojection error (< ~0.5 px). Re-calibrate when focus or resolution changes.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is hand–eye calibration?
notes.back:
Finding the fixed transform between a camera and the robot so that detections can be expressed in the robot base frame.

• Eye-in-hand: camera on the end-effector → solve camera-to-flange.
• Eye-to-hand: static camera → solve camera-to-base.

Move the arm to many poses while viewing a calibration target and solve AX = XB (Tsai–Lenz, Park–Martin; cv2.calibrateHandEye).
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Stereo vision: give the depth equation and the error behaviour.
notes.back:
For rectified cameras: Z = f·B / d
f = focal length (pixels), B = baseline, d = disparity (pixels).

Depth uncertainty grows quadratically with range: δZ ≈ Z²/(f·B) · δd. → A wider baseline or longer focal length improves far-range accuracy but increases the minimum range.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How do classical visual pipelines find correspondences between images?
notes.back:
Detect key-points → describe → match → reject outliers.

• Detectors/descriptors: SIFT (accurate, slow), ORB = Oriented FAST + Rotated BRIEF (binary, real-time; used in ORB-SLAM).
• Matching: nearest neighbour + ratio test.
• Outliers: Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) fitting an essential/fundamental matrix or homography.

Learned replacements: SuperPoint + SuperGlue/LightGlue.
notes.source: Hartley & Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry (2nd ed.); OpenCV calibration docs — https://docs.opencv.org/ · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What are fiducial markers (AprilTag, ArUco) used for?
notes.back:
Printed binary-coded squares that are trivial to detect robustly. With known tag size and camera intrinsics, a single tag yields the full 6-DoF camera-to-tag pose (Perspective-n-Point).

Uses: ground-truth localisation, docking, hand–eye and multi-camera calibration, object tracking in data collection rigs.
notes.source: AprilTag (Olson 2011; Wang & Olson 2016) — https://april.eecs.umich.edu/software/apriltag · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Describe the Bayes filter, the template behind all recursive state estimators.
notes.back:
Maintain a belief bel(xt) and alternate:
Predict (motion model, control u): bel⁻(xt) = ∫ p(xt | ut, xt−1) bel(xt−1) dxt−1 — uncertainty grows.
Update (measurement z): bel(xt) = η · p(zt | xt) · bel⁻(xt) — uncertainty shrinks.

Assumes the Markov property. Kalman filter = Gaussian beliefs; particle filter = samples; histogram filter = grid.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Write the Kalman filter equations.
notes.back:
Predict
x̂⁻ = A·x̂ + B·u
P⁻ = A·P·Aᵀ + Q
Update
K = P⁻Hᵀ(H·P⁻Hᵀ + R)⁻¹
x̂ = x̂⁻ + K·(z − H·x̂⁻)
P = (I − K·H)·P⁻

Q = process noise, R = measurement noise. The Kalman gain K weights prediction against measurement by their uncertainties. Optimal for linear systems with Gaussian noise.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) vs. Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF).
notes.back:
Both handle non-linear models xt = f(x,u), z = h(x).

EKF: linearise f and h with Jacobians at the current estimate; cheap; can diverge when strongly non-linear or badly initialised.
UKF: propagate deterministically chosen sigma points through the true non-linear functions and recover mean/covariance; no Jacobians, usually more accurate at similar cost.

ROS example: robot_localization fuses wheel odometry + IMU (+ GNSS) with either.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is a particle filter, and what is Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization (AMCL)?
notes.back:
Represent the belief by N weighted samples (particles): move each with the noisy motion model → weight by measurement likelihood → resample in proportion to weight.

+ Handles multi-modal, non-Gaussian beliefs → global localisation and the 'kidnapped robot' problem.
− Cost grows with state dimension.

AMCL: particle-filter localisation of a 2D LiDAR robot in a known occupancy map, adapting the particle count (KLD sampling). Default localiser in Nav2.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Define Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and say why it is hard.
notes.back:
Estimating the robot's trajectory and a map of an unknown environment at the same time.

Chicken-and-egg: a map is needed to localise, and poses are needed to build a map. Both errors are correlated, odometry drifts, and data association (is this the same place/landmark?) can fail catastrophically.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation
