notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: In modern graph-based SLAM, what do the front-end and back-end do, and what is loop closure?
notes.back:
Front-end: turns raw sensor data into constraints — odometry / scan matching / visual feature tracking, and place recognition.
Back-end: non-linear least-squares optimisation of a pose graph or factor graph (nodes = poses/landmarks, edges = relative measurements) — g2o, GTSAM, Ceres.

Loop closure: recognising a previously visited place adds an edge that lets the optimiser cancel accumulated drift. False loop closures wreck the map → robust kernels and verification.
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is an occupancy grid map?
notes.back:
A 2D (or 3D voxel — OctoMap) grid in which each cell stores the probability of being occupied, updated per range beam with an inverse sensor model, usually in log-odds form so that updates are additions: l ← l + lmeas − l0.

Assumes cells are independent and poses are known. It is the map format consumed by ROS 2 navigation (costmaps).
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is Iterative Closest Point (ICP)?
notes.back:
Aligns two point clouds/scans: repeat {match each point to its nearest neighbour in the other cloud → solve the rigid transform minimising the distances (closed-form via SVD) → apply} until convergence.

Needs a good initial guess (local minima); point-to-plane and Generalized ICP converge better; Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) is a common alternative. Core of LiDAR odometry and scan matching; pre-process with voxel down-sampling and outlier removal (PCL, Open3D).
notes.source: Thrun, Burgard & Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Visual Odometry (VO) and Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO): what are they, and what is the monocular scale problem?
notes.back:
VO estimates camera motion from image sequences (feature-based or direct). With a single camera, translation is recovered only up to an unknown scale, and the scale drifts.

VIO tightly fuses an IMU: metric scale and gravity direction become observable, and fast motions/short visual drop-outs are bridged. Examples: VINS-Fusion, OpenVINS, ORB-SLAM3 (mono/stereo/RGB-D + inertial, multi-map); the principle behind AR/VR headset and drone tracking.
notes.source: Campos et al. 2021, ORB-SLAM3 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.11898 · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: Object detection vs. semantic segmentation vs. instance segmentation vs. 6D pose estimation.
notes.back:
Detection: class + bounding box per object (e.g. YOLO family).
Semantic segmentation: class label per pixel, no object identities.
Instance segmentation: a separate mask per object (Mask R-CNN; promptable: Segment Anything).
6D pose estimation: 3D position + 3D orientation of a known (or novel) object — what classical grasp planning needs (e.g. FoundationPose).
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: How have vision foundation models changed robot perception?
notes.back:
Pre-trained encoders replace task-specific training:
• CLIP / SigLIP — image–text aligned features → open-vocabulary recognition.
• DINOv2 — self-supervised dense features with strong geometry/correspondence.
• Segment Anything (SAM), Grounding DINO / OWL-ViT — promptable, open-vocabulary segmentation and detection.
• Monocular depth (Depth Anything).

SigLIP + DINOv2 is the most common vision front-end of Vision-Language-Action models (e.g. OpenVLA).
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::09 Perception & State Estimation
notes.front: What is Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) positioning?
notes.back:
A Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) technique: a fixed base station at a known location (or a network service via NTRIP) streams carrier-phase corrections to the rover, which resolves the integer carrier ambiguities → centimetre-level position instead of metres.

Needs open sky and a correction link; heading requires motion or a dual-antenna set-up. Standard for agricultural robots, survey drones and outdoor ground robots.
notes.source: Siegwart, Nourbakhsh & Scaramuzza, Introduction to Autonomous Mobile Robots (2nd ed.) · 09 Perception & State Estimation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Path planning vs. trajectory planning vs. control.
notes.back:
Path: a purely geometric curve q(s) from start to goal, collision-free.
Trajectory: the path plus timing, q(t), respecting velocity/acceleration/jerk/torque limits.
Control: tracking the trajectory with feedback despite disturbances.
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Dijkstra vs. A* on a grid or graph.
notes.back:
Dijkstra expands nodes in order of cost-so-far g(n) → optimal but explores in all directions.
A* orders by f(n) = g(n) + h(n), with h a heuristic estimate of the cost-to-go. If h is admissible (never overestimates — e.g. Euclidean distance) A* is optimal; if also consistent, no node is re-expanded. h = 0 reduces A* to Dijkstra.

Variants: Theta* (any-angle), D* Lite (re-planning), Hybrid-A* (car-like kinematics).
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Why do arm planners sample configuration space instead of searching a grid?
notes.back:
A grid over an n-joint C-space has resolutionⁿ cells (curse of dimensionality), and C-space obstacles have no explicit description — only a collision checker is available.

Sampling-based planners just test random configurations for collision. They are probabilistically complete: the probability of finding an existing solution → 1 with more samples, but they cannot prove that none exists.
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Probabilistic Roadmap (PRM) vs. Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT).
notes.back:
PRM — multi-query: sample many collision-free configurations, connect neighbours with collision-free local paths into a roadmap, then graph-search it. Good for static scenes.
RRT — single-query: grow a tree from the start by steering the nearest node a step toward a random sample (with some goal bias); rapidly explores high-dimensional and kinodynamic spaces. RRT-Connect grows two trees.
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: What does RRT* add to RRT?
notes.back: Asymptotic optimality: each new node chooses the lowest-cost parent within a shrinking radius and then rewires neighbours through itself when that is cheaper → path cost converges to the optimum as samples → ∞ (plain RRT almost surely does not). Informed RRT* and BIT* focus sampling to converge faster. In practice planners' paths are also shortcut/smoothed afterwards. Library: Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL).
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: How is a geometric path turned into a smooth joint trajectory?
notes.back:
Time-parameterisation under limits:
• Trapezoidal velocity profile — accelerate, cruise, decelerate (bang-coast-bang); S-curve adds jerk limits.
• Polynomials — cubic (match position + velocity), quintic (also acceleration) between way-points; splines through many.
• Time-optimal parameterisation along a fixed path (TOPP-RA; MoveIt ships Time-Optimal Trajectory Generation and the jerk-limited Ruckig).
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Global planner, local planner (controller) and costmaps in mobile-robot navigation.
notes.back:
Global planner: route over the whole map (A*, Dijkstra, Hybrid-A*/Smac), re-planned occasionally.
Local planner / controller: at 10–20+ Hz turns the route plus live sensor data into velocity commands, avoiding dynamic obstacles.
Costmaps: layered grids (static map, obstacle, inflation layer that pads obstacles by the robot radius with decaying cost) — one global, one rolling local window.
notes.source: Nav2 documentation — https://docs.nav2.org/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control: how do these local planners work?
notes.back:
DWA: sample (v, ω) pairs reachable within one time-step given acceleration limits (the 'dynamic window'), forward-simulate each briefly, discard colliding ones, pick the best score (goal heading, clearance, speed).
MPPI: sample thousands of noisy control sequences over a horizon, roll them out through the model, and average them weighted by exp(−cost) — a sampling-based MPC that handles non-convex costs; widely used in Nav2.
notes.source: Nav2 documentation — https://docs.nav2.org/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Pure pursuit path tracking.
notes.back:
Pick a goal point on the path one look-ahead distance Ld ahead; steer along the circular arc through it:
κ = 2·y / Ld² (y = lateral offset of the goal point in the robot frame); ω = v·κ.

Short Ld → accurate but oscillatory; long Ld → smooth but cuts corners. Commonly scaled with speed (Nav2 Regulated Pure Pursuit). Stanley control is the front-axle alternative for cars.
notes.source: Nav2 documentation — https://docs.nav2.org/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Artificial potential fields: idea and fatal flaw.
notes.back:
The goal exerts an attractive potential, obstacles a repulsive one; the robot follows the negative gradient. Reactive, cheap, smooth.

Flaw: local minima (e.g. U-shaped obstacles, goal behind a wall) and oscillation in narrow corridors. Hence used as a local reactive layer or replaced by navigation functions / planners with global information.
notes.source: LaValle, Planning Algorithms — https://lavalle.pl/planning/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Why have Behavior Trees (BTs) displaced Finite State Machines for robot task logic?
notes.back:
A BT is a tree ticked from the root at a fixed rate; every node returns SUCCESS, FAILURE or RUNNING.
• Sequence (→): run children in order until one fails.
• Fallback/Selector (?): try children until one succeeds → built-in recovery behaviours.
• Decorators, conditions, actions.

Versus FSMs: modular and reusable sub-trees, no transition explosion, inherently reactive (conditions re-checked every tick). Nav2's navigator is a BT (BehaviorTree.CPP, XML-defined).
notes.source: Colledanchise & Ögren, Behavior Trees in Robotics and AI — https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.00084 · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Sampling-based planning vs. trajectory optimisation for manipulators.
notes.back:
Sampling-based (RRT-Connect, PRM): global exploration, probabilistic completeness, jerky paths needing post-processing; handles narrow passages poorly but does not get stuck in local minima.
Trajectory optimisation (CHOMP, STOMP, TrajOpt; GPU-parallel cuRobo): minimise smoothness + collision cost over the whole trajectory; fast and smooth, but local — depends on the initial guess.

Common combination: sample to find a seed, optimise to refine. Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) adds a symbolic layer above for long-horizon tasks.
notes.source: MoveIt 2 documentation — https://moveit.picknik.ai/ · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::10 Motion Planning & Navigation
notes.front: Classical grasp planning: what is force closure, and how do modern data-driven grasp planners differ?
notes.back:
Force closure: the contact forces (within friction cones) can resist an arbitrary external wrench; for a parallel-jaw gripper this reduces to an antipodal grasp — contact normals roughly opposed and inside each other's friction cone. Needs an object model and pose.

Data-driven: networks predict grasp poses and quality directly from a depth image or point cloud of unknown objects (Dex-Net, GraspNet, Contact-GraspNet) — no model required. End-to-end visuomotor policies go further and skip explicit grasp planning.
notes.source: Lynch & Park, Modern Robotics (2017) — http://modernrobotics.org · 10 Motion Planning & Navigation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is the Robot Operating System (ROS), and what is the status of ROS 1?
notes.back:
Not an operating system: open-source middleware + tools + libraries — message passing between processes, hardware drivers, visualisation (RViz), logging, build tooling, and packages for navigation, manipulation and perception.

ROS 1's final release, Noetic, reached end-of-life on 31 May 2025. New work uses ROS 2: no central master, built on DDS, real-time and multi-robot capable, security, lifecycle nodes, Windows/macOS support.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: ROS 2 communication primitives: node, topic, service, action.
notes.back:
Node: a process-level unit of computation.
Topic: typed, anonymous publish/subscribe stream — many-to-many (sensor data, cmd_vel).
Service: synchronous-style request/response for quick queries.
Action: long-running, pre-emptable goal with periodic feedback and a final result (navigate to pose, follow joint trajectory).
Plus parameters for run-time configuration.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is the Data Distribution Service (DDS) in ROS 2, and what is the RMW layer?
notes.back:
DDS is an industrial publish/subscribe standard with automatic peer discovery (no ROS master), transported over UDP with the RTPS wire protocol, and rich Quality of Service.

The ROS Middleware (RMW) interface abstracts the vendor: Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, RTI Connext — and, since recent distributions, the non-DDS Zenoh (rmw_zenoh), which behaves better over Wi-Fi and wide-area links. ROS_DOMAIN_ID isolates robots on a shared network.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Which Quality of Service (QoS) settings matter most in ROS 2, and what is the classic pitfall?
notes.back:
• Reliability: RELIABLE (retransmit) vs. BEST_EFFORT (drop; right for high-rate sensor data on lossy links).
• Durability: VOLATILE vs. TRANSIENT_LOCAL (late joiners receive the last message — used for maps, /robot_description).
• History/depth: queue size.
• Deadline, liveliness.

Pitfall: incompatible QoS = silently no data — e.g. a RELIABLE subscriber will not match a BEST_EFFORT publisher. Check with ros2 topic info -v.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Which ROS 2 distributions are supported as of mid-2026, and which should a new project choose?
notes.back:
• Lyrical Luth — released 22 May 2026, Long-Term Support (LTS) until May 2031.
• Kilted Kaiju — May 2025, non-LTS, end-of-life December 2026.
• Jazzy Jalisco — May 2024, LTS until May 2029 (Ubuntu 24.04).
• Humble Hawksbill — May 2022, LTS until May 2027 (Ubuntu 22.04).
• Rolling Ridley — continuous development branch.

Pattern: a release every May; even years are LTS tied to the Ubuntu LTS. New projects: the newest LTS that your drivers/dependencies already support.
notes.source: ROS 2 distributions list — https://docs.ros.org/en/rolling/Releases.html · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: tf2 and REP 105: what is the standard frame chain of a mobile robot and who publishes each link?
notes.back:
map → odom → base_link → (sensor frames)

• odom → base_link: from odometry/IMU fusion. Continuous and smooth, but drifts.
• map → odom: from localisation/SLAM (AMCL, SLAM Toolbox). Globally accurate, may jump.
• base_link → sensors: static transforms from the URDF via robot_state_publisher.

tf2 maintains this time-stamped tree (each frame has exactly one parent) and answers 'transform between any two frames at time t'. Conventions: x forward, y left, z up; SI units (REP 103).
notes.source: REP 105, Coordinate Frames for Mobile Platforms — https://www.ros.org/reps/rep-0105.html · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) file?
notes.back:
An XML description of the robot as a tree of links (visual mesh, collision geometry, inertial properties) connected by joints (fixed, revolute, continuous, prismatic; axis, limits).

Consumers: robot_state_publisher (tf), RViz, MoveIt, ros2_control, simulators. xacro adds macros and parameters. Limitations: tree only (no closed kinematic loops), one robot — Gazebo's SDF and MuJoCo's MJCF are richer; OpenUSD is used in Isaac Sim.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is ros2_control?
notes.back:
The real-time control framework of ROS 2:
• Hardware interface plugins expose state (position, velocity, effort) and command interfaces for real or simulated hardware.
• The controller manager runs a deterministic read → update → write loop.
• Swappable controllers: joint_trajectory_controller, diff_drive_controller, joint_state_broadcaster, admittance, PID …

The same controllers run on Gazebo, a mock system or the real robot — MoveIt and Nav2 sit on top.
notes.source: ros2_control documentation — https://control.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Name the main components of the Nav2 navigation stack.
notes.back:
• BT Navigator — a behaviour tree orchestrating the task.
• Planner server — global path (NavFn, Smac Hybrid-A*/lattice, Theta*).
• Controller server — path following (MPPI, Regulated Pure Pursuit, DWB).
• Costmap 2D — global and local layered costmaps.
• Behaviour server — recoveries (spin, back up, wait); smoother server; waypoint follower; collision monitor.
• Localisation: AMCL with a map server, or SLAM Toolbox.
• Lifecycle manager brings the managed nodes up in order.
notes.source: Nav2 documentation — https://docs.nav2.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What does MoveIt 2 provide?
notes.back:
The ROS 2 manipulation framework:
• Planning scene — world + robot model, collision checking (FCL/Bullet), attached objects, octomap from depth sensors.
• Motion planning plugins — OMPL (sampling), Pilz industrial planner (PTP/LIN/CIRC), STOMP/CHOMP.
• IK plugins — KDL, TRAC-IK, IKFast, pick_ik.
• Time parameterisation (TOTG, Ruckig), execution through ros2_control.
• MoveIt Servo for real-time Cartesian jogging/tele-operation; MoveIt Task Constructor for multi-stage pick-and-place.
notes.source: MoveIt 2 documentation — https://moveit.picknik.ai/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is micro-ROS?
notes.back:
ROS 2 for microcontrollers: a client library (rclc) on top of Micro XRCE-DDS, running on an RTOS (FreeRTOS, Zephyr, NuttX) or bare-metal Arduino-style targets — ESP32, STM32, Teensy, Raspberry Pi Pico.

The microcontroller connects over serial/USB/UDP/CAN to a micro-ROS Agent on the Linux host, which bridges it into the ROS 2 graph — so the motor controller becomes a first-class node with publishers, subscribers, services and parameters.
notes.source: micro-ROS — https://micro.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: What is rosbag2 and why is it central to robotics development?
notes.back:
Records and replays any set of topics with timestamps (ros2 bag record -a, ros2 bag play). Default storage format is MCAP (since Iron).

Uses: debug offline, tune perception/SLAM repeatably on identical data, regression-test algorithms, build datasets, replay with use_sim_time. Visualise with RViz, Foxglove or PlotJuggler.
notes.source: ROS 2 Documentation — https://docs.ros.org/ · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::11 ROS 2 & Simulation
notes.front: Compare the main robotics simulators: Gazebo, MuJoCo, Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab, and Newton.
notes.back:
Gazebo (modern 'gz'; Gazebo Classic reached end-of-life in January 2025): the ROS-integrated general simulator — sensors, worlds, ros2_control; full-system and navigation testing.
MuJoCo (DeepMind, open-source since 2022): fast, accurate articulated-body and contact dynamics; the research standard for control and reinforcement learning; GPU variants MJX and MuJoCo Warp.
NVIDIA Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab: GPU PhysX + ray-traced rendering on OpenUSD; thousands of parallel environments for reinforcement learning and synthetic data.
Newton: open-source GPU physics engine built on NVIDIA Warp, co-developed by NVIDIA, Google DeepMind and Disney Research (announced 2025), differentiable and aimed at robot learning.
notes.source: Gazebo https://gazebosim.org/ · MuJoCo https://mujoco.org/ · Isaac Lab https://isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab/ · Newton https://github.com/newton-physics/newton · 11 ROS 2 & Simulation

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: Define a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and say why real robots are actually POMDPs.
notes.back:
MDP = (S, A, P, R, γ): states, actions, transition probabilities P(s′|s,a), reward, discount. Goal: a policy π(a|s) maximising the expected discounted return Σ γtrt.

A robot never sees the true state — only camera images and joint readings — so it faces a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP). Practical answers: feed the policy a history of observations, a recurrent/transformer memory, or an estimated state.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.) — http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: Reinforcement Learning (RL) vs. Imitation Learning (IL) for robots: trade-offs.
notes.back:
RL: learns from reward by trial and error. + Can exceed human skill, discovers recovery behaviour. − Sample-hungry, unsafe on hardware, reward design is hard → mostly done in simulation. Dominant for locomotion.
IL: supervised learning from demonstrations. + No reward or simulator needed, works from real images. − Bounded by demonstration quality/coverage, data is costly. Dominant for manipulation.

Frontier practice combines them: pre-train by imitation, improve with RL.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.) — http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is Behaviour Cloning (BC) and what is its fundamental failure mode?
notes.back:
BC = supervised regression from observation to the expert's action.

Failure mode: covariate shift / compounding error. Small mistakes take the robot to states the expert never visited; there the policy is worse, errors grow — for naive BC the expected error scales O(T²) with horizon T.

Mitigations: more diverse data including recoveries, DAgger-style corrections, action chunking, noise injection during demonstration, expressive (diffusion/flow) policies.
notes.source: Ross, Gordon & Bagnell 2011, DAgger — https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0686 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: How does Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) fix behaviour cloning's distribution shift?
notes.back:
Iterate: (1) run the current learner policy to collect the states it visits; (2) ask the expert to label those states with the correct action; (3) add them to the dataset and retrain.

The training distribution converges to the learner's own state distribution → error grows linearly rather than quadratically with horizon. Robotics variants: human-gated interventions (HG-DAgger) — the operator takes over only when the robot is about to fail, and those corrections become training data.
notes.source: Ross, Gordon & Bagnell 2011, DAgger — https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.0686 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) vs. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC): what are they and where is each used in robotics?
notes.back:
PPO — on-policy policy gradient with a clipped surrogate objective that limits each update's policy change; stable, simple, scales across thousands of parallel simulated environments → the standard for sim-trained locomotion and whole-body control.
SAC — off-policy actor-critic with a replay buffer and an entropy bonus (maximum-entropy RL); far more sample-efficient → preferred for learning directly on real robots.
notes.source: Schulman et al. 2017, PPO — https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347 · Haarnoja et al. 2018, SAC — https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.01290 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What are reward shaping and reward hacking?
notes.back:
Shaping: adding dense intermediate terms (distance to goal, velocity tracking, energy, smoothness penalties) because sparse success/failure rewards make exploration hopeless. Locomotion rewards typically have 10–20 weighted terms.
Hacking: the agent maximises the written reward in an unintended way (vibrating forward, exploiting simulator bugs).

Alternatives: motion-imitation/tracking rewards from human or animal motion capture, learned reward models, or sparse reward + demonstrations.
notes.source: Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction (2nd ed.) — http://incompleteideas.net/book/the-book-2nd.html · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is the sim-to-real gap and where does it come from?
notes.back:
A policy that works in simulation fails on hardware because the simulator is wrong or incomplete about:
• Dynamics: mass/inertia, friction, contact and deformable objects.
• Actuators: torque limits, gear friction/backlash, bandwidth, latency.
• Sensing: noise, bias, delays, calibration.
• Visuals: rendering vs. real cameras, lighting, clutter.

Remedies: system identification, domain randomisation, learned actuator models, online adaptation, and real-world fine-tuning.
notes.source: Tobin et al. 2017, Domain Randomization — https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is domain randomisation?
notes.back:
Train across a wide distribution of simulators instead of one: randomise physics (masses, friction, motor strength, delays, push disturbances) and/or visuals (textures, lighting, camera pose) every episode.

The real world then looks like just another sample, and the policy is forced to be robust or to adapt implicitly. Too little randomisation → no transfer; too much → over-conservative behaviour. It is the main reason RL locomotion policies transfer zero-shot.
notes.source: Tobin et al. 2017, Domain Randomization — https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06907 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is an 'actuator network', and why did it matter for legged-robot RL?
notes.back:
A small neural network trained on real hardware logs to predict the torque a joint actuator actually produces from its recent history of commanded and measured positions/velocities — capturing friction, compliance, controller dynamics and delay that analytic models miss.

Inserted into the simulator, it closed the sim-to-real gap for ANYmal (Hwangbo et al., Science Robotics 2019) and enabled zero-shot transfer of RL locomotion policies.
notes.source: Hwangbo et al. 2019, Learning agile and dynamic motor skills for legged robots (Science Robotics) — https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08652 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: Explain teacher–student (privileged) learning and Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA).
notes.back:
Teacher: trained with RL in simulation with privileged information the real robot lacks (terrain friction, height map, payload, contact states).
Student: uses only on-board sensors; learns by supervised learning to imitate the teacher or to infer the privileged latent from a history of proprioception.

RMA: base policy conditioned on an 'extrinsics' latent + an adaptation module estimating that latent online from recent states/actions → adapts to new terrain and payloads within fractions of a second, with no real-world fine-tuning.
notes.source: Kumar et al. 2021, RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation — https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.04034 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: Why did massively parallel GPU simulation change robot reinforcement learning?
notes.back:
Physics and the neural network both run on the GPU, so thousands of environments step in parallel with no CPU–GPU transfer. Rudin et al. (2021) trained quadruped locomotion with ~4000 parallel robots in minutes (flat terrain) to ~20 minutes (rough terrain) on a single GPU; a terrain curriculum raises difficulty automatically.

Tools: Isaac Gym → Isaac Lab, MuJoCo MJX / MuJoCo Warp, Genesis, ManiSkill. Industrial example: Figure's Helix 02 low-level controller was trained across more than 200 000 parallel environments.
notes.source: Rudin et al. 2021, Learning to Walk in Minutes — https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.11978 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is action chunking, as used in Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)?
notes.back:
The policy predicts a sequence of the next k actions per inference (e.g. k ≈ 50–100 at 50 Hz) instead of one.

Why: shortens the effective decision horizon → less compounding error; copes with non-Markovian demonstration quirks such as pauses; yields smooth motion. ACT adds a conditional Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) to model demonstration variability and temporal ensembling (average overlapping chunks). Introduced with the low-cost bimanual ALOHA system; chunking is now used by virtually all Vision-Language-Action models.
notes.source: Zhao et al. 2023, ALOHA / Action Chunking with Transformers — https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.13705 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: What is Diffusion Policy and which problem of behaviour cloning does it solve?
notes.back:
The policy generates an action sequence by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, conditioned on recent observations (conditional DDPM); part of the sequence is executed, then it re-plans (receding horizon).

Solves multi-modality: humans demonstrate the same task in different ways (pass left or right). A regression policy averages the modes — an invalid action; a diffusion model represents the full distribution and commits to one mode. Also trains stably and scales to high-dimensional action sequences.
notes.source: Chi et al. 2023, Diffusion Policy — https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::12 Robot Learning Foundations
notes.front: How is demonstration data for manipulation policies collected?
notes.back:
• Leader–follower tele-operation: the operator moves a kinematic replica arm; the robot mirrors it (ALOHA, GELLO, SO-101). Intuitive; joint-space data.
• Virtual-reality / hand tracking (Apple Vision Pro, Quest): maps hand poses to arms and dexterous hands; standard for humanoids.
• Robot-free hand-held grippers — Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI): instrumented gripper with a camera; trajectories recovered by visual SLAM; data collected anywhere.
• Egocentric human video (smart glasses): most scalable, but no action labels.
• Kinesthetic teaching; 3D mouse. Quality, diversity and recoveries matter more than sheer volume.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 12 Robot Learning Foundations

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is meant by 'Physical AI' / 'embodied AI'?
notes.back:
AI systems that perceive, reason about and act in the physical world through a body — robots, vehicles, drones — rather than only processing digital content. The defining requirement is closing the loop from raw sensors (pixels, touch, proprioception) to motor commands under real-world physics, real time and safety constraints.

Current paradigm: large pre-trained foundation models (vision-language-action models, world models) + simulation/synthetic data + fleet data, replacing hand-engineered perception–planning–control pipelines for unstructured tasks.
notes.source: NVIDIA 2025, Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03575 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: State Moravec's paradox and its consequence for robotics.
notes.back:
'It is comparatively easy to make computers exhibit adult-level performance on intelligence tests or playing checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the skills of a one-year-old when it comes to perception and mobility.'

Sensorimotor skill is the product of hundreds of millions of years of evolution and is largely unconscious, so it is hard to specify — and unlike text, no internet-scale dataset of robot actions exists. This data gap is the central bottleneck of Physical AI.
notes.source: Moravec 1988, Mind Children · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Define a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model.
notes.back:
A model that takes visual observations and a natural-language instruction as required inputs (optionally proprioception, depth, touch) and directly outputs robot control commands. Typically a pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone — bringing web-scale semantic knowledge — plus an action output mechanism (discrete action tokens, or a diffusion / flow-matching head).

Systems where a language model merely selects among pre-trained skills (e.g. SayCan) are not VLAs under this definition.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: RT-1 → RT-2: what was the key idea of Robotics Transformer 2?
notes.back:
RT-1 (2022): a transformer trained from scratch on ~130 000 real demonstrations of 700+ tasks — a capable multi-task policy, but it only knows what is in the robot data.

RT-2 (2023): take a large web-pre-trained VLM (PaLI-X / PaLM-E), write robot actions as text tokens, and co-fine-tune on web vision-language data + robot data. Result: semantic generalisation absent from the robot data ('pick up the extinct animal', unseen objects) — web knowledge transfers to control. This coined the term VLA.
notes.source: Brohan et al. 2023, RT-2 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15818 (RT-1: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06817) · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: How do autoregressive VLAs turn continuous actions into tokens, what is the drawback, and what does the FAST tokenizer change?
notes.back:
Binning: each action dimension per time-step is discretised into 256 bins → one token each (RT-2, OpenVLA), trained with next-token cross-entropy.
Drawback: many highly correlated tokens at high control rates → slow inference and poor learning of dexterous, high-frequency tasks.

FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization): apply a Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) to each action chunk, quantise, then compress with Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) → far fewer tokens; about 5× faster training and autoregressive VLAs that match diffusion-style models on dexterous tasks.
notes.source: Pertsch et al. 2025, FAST action tokenizer — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09747 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is the Open X-Embodiment (OXE) dataset and what did it demonstrate?
notes.back:
A pooled, standardised collection of 60 existing robot datasets from 21 institutions: 1M+ real trajectories, 22 robot embodiments, 500+ skills (RLDS format).

Finding (RT-X models): a single policy trained on the mixture outperforms policies trained only on each lab's own data — positive transfer across embodiments. It became the default pre-training corpus for open generalist policies (Octo, OpenVLA). Open issue: differing action spaces, cameras and control rates make cross-embodiment learning hard.
notes.source: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration 2023 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08864 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: OpenVLA: architecture and significance.
notes.back:
7B-parameter open-source VLA (2024): Llama 2 language model + fused SigLIP and DINOv2 vision encoders (Prismatic VLM), outputs 256-bin discrete action tokens; trained on 970 000 Open X-Embodiment episodes.

Outperformed the closed 55B RT-2-X with 7× fewer parameters, and showed practical adaptation with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning and quantisation on consumer GPUs. Follow-up OpenVLA-OFT: parallel decoding of continuous action chunks for much higher speed.
notes.source: Kim et al. 2024, OpenVLA — https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09246 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: π0 (Physical Intelligence, 2024): what is the architecture?
notes.back:
A pre-trained VLM (PaliGemma, ~3B) plus a separate ~300M-parameter action expert — a second set of transformer weights attending to the same sequence — that generates continuous action chunks by flow matching, enabling control at up to 50 Hz for dexterous tasks (laundry folding, box assembly, table bussing).

Recipe borrowed from language models: pre-train on large, diverse cross-embodiment data (~10 000 hours, several robot types), then post-train on smaller, high-quality task data. Weights are open-sourced (openpi).
notes.source: Black et al. 2024, π0 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Flow matching vs. diffusion for action generation.
notes.back:
Both map noise to data conditioned on observations. Diffusion learns to reverse a stochastic noising process over many denoising steps. Flow matching directly regresses a velocity field that transports noise samples to data along (near-)straight paths; at inference you integrate an ordinary differential equation.

Simpler training objective and good samples in ~5–10 integration steps → low latency, which matters for high-rate control. Used by π0, GR00T N1 and successors.
notes.source: Lipman et al. 2022, Flow Matching — https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is the 'System 1 / System 2' dual-system VLA architecture?
notes.back:
Borrowing Kahneman's terms:
System 2 — a large VLM that reasons about the scene and the instruction, slowly (a few Hz), and emits a latent/semantic conditioning.
System 1 — a small, fast visuomotor policy that turns that conditioning + fresh observations into continuous actions at control rate.

Example: Figure Helix — S2 ≈ 7B parameters at 7–9 Hz; S1 ≈ 80M parameters at 200 Hz controlling a 35-DoF humanoid upper body, running asynchronously on on-board GPUs. NVIDIA GR00T N1 uses the same split (VLM + diffusion-transformer action module). It resolves the 'general but slow vs. fast but narrow' trade-off.
notes.source: Figure AI, Helix — https://www.figure.ai/news/helix · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Helix 02 (Figure, January 2026): what is 'System 0'?
notes.back:
Helix 02 extends the S1/S2 hierarchy to full-body autonomy with a third, lowest layer:
S0 — a ~10M-parameter network running at 1 kHz that takes full-body joint state and base motion and outputs joint-level actuator commands, handling balance, contact and coordination. It is a learned whole-body controller trained to track human motion data, entirely in simulation (>200 000 parallel environments, heavy domain randomisation).
S1 — 'all sensors in, all joints out' (head and palm cameras, fingertip tactile, proprioception) at 200 Hz.
S2 — slow semantic reasoning.

Pattern: pixels-to-torque hierarchy, each layer at its natural time-scale.
notes.source: Figure AI, Helix 02 (Jan 2026) — https://www.figure.ai/news/helix-02 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: π0.5 (2025): what did it add over π0?
notes.back:
Open-world generalisation: cleaning kitchens and bedrooms in homes never seen in training, on a mobile manipulator.

How: co-training on heterogeneous data — many robot types, web vision-language data, object detection, verbal instructions — and a hierarchical inference inside one model: first predict a high-level sub-task in language ('pick up the plate'), then generate the low-level action chunk by flow matching. Discrete FAST tokens are used in pre-training, the continuous flow action expert in post-training.
notes.source: Physical Intelligence 2025, π0.5 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: π0.7 (Physical Intelligence, April 2026): what is 'diverse context conditioning' and what does it buy?
notes.back:
A ~5B VLA: Gemma 3 4B VLM backbone + video-history (memory) encoder + ~860M flow-matching action expert.

Key idea: during training the prompt contains not only what to do (language) but also how: episode metadata describing data quality and strategy, and sub-goal images. This disambiguates mixed-quality data, so the model can learn from demonstrations, sub-optimal autonomous roll-outs including failures, and non-robot data — then be steered at test time towards fast, high-quality behaviour.

Reported results: strong out-of-the-box performance without task-specific fine-tuning, matching RL-fine-tuned specialists on hard tasks; signs of compositional generalisation; zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer.
notes.source: Physical Intelligence 2026, π0.7 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15483 · https://www.pi.website/blog/pi07 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N-series: what is it, and what changed by N1.7 (2026)?
notes.back:
An open VLA foundation model family for humanoid / generalist robots. GR00T N1 (March 2025): dual-system — VLM 'System 2' + diffusion-transformer 'System 1' action head with flow matching; cross-embodiment; trained on a mix of real tele-operation, human video (via latent actions) and synthetic data; post-trainable per robot.

N1.7 (2026): new VLM backbone Cosmos-Reason2-2B (Qwen3-VL architecture, native-aspect-ratio images), larger state/action dimensions and action horizon, multi-dataset fine-tuning with mixture weights; commercially usable licence. Ecosystem: Isaac Sim/Lab, Cosmos world models, Jetson Thor on-board compute, and an open reference humanoid design.
notes.source: NVIDIA Isaac GR00T — https://github.com/NVIDIA/Isaac-GR00T · GR00T N1 paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14734 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Gemini Robotics 1.5 (Google DeepMind): what are the two models and the three headline ideas?
notes.back:
Gemini Robotics-ER 1.5 — an Embodied Reasoning VLM: spatial understanding, pointing, task planning, progress/success estimation; it orchestrates (and can call tools such as search).
Gemini Robotics 1.5 — the VLA that executes each step.

Ideas: (1) Motion Transfer — an architecture/training recipe for learning from heterogeneous multi-embodiment data; skills shown on ALOHA transfer to a bi-arm Franka and the Apollo humanoid without robot-specific post-training. (2) Thinking before acting — the VLA interleaves natural-language reasoning with actions (embodied chain-of-thought): better multi-step performance and interpretability. (3) An agentic system combining both models, with semantic-safety evaluation (ASIMOV benchmark).
notes.source: Gemini Robotics Team 2025, Gemini Robotics 1.5 — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03342 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is a world (foundation) model in Physical AI, and what is it used for?
notes.back:
A generative model that predicts future observations (usually video, sometimes latent states) given the current observation and, ideally, actions — a learned simulator of visual physics. Example platform: NVIDIA Cosmos (Predict, Transfer, Reason models; Cosmos 3 announced in 2026).

Uses: (1) synthetic data — multiply and re-style demonstrations, render sim data photoreal; (2) policy evaluation in imagination; (3) planning / model-based control; (4) pre-training representations for policies. Limitation: long-horizon physical and action-conditional consistency.
notes.source: NVIDIA 2025, Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI — https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03575 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is the 2026 trend from VLAs towards 'world-action models' / video-model policies?
notes.back:
Instead of bolting an action head onto a vision-language model, start from a pre-trained video generation model — which already encodes dynamics and physics — and train it to predict future frames and actions jointly (actions as an extra modality in the latent sequence, or decoded by an inverse-dynamics model from predicted video).

Motivation: video pre-training carries motion priors that static image–text pre-training lacks, and imagined futures enable planning and value estimation. Examples: Unified Video Action model, DreamGen, Cosmos Policy, DreamZero. Open question: inference cost at control rate.
notes.source: Curated paper list: awesome-physical-ai — https://github.com/keon/awesome-physical-ai · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What is the 'data pyramid' for training robot foundation models?
notes.back:
From scarce-and-relevant to abundant-and-indirect:
1. Real robot tele-operation — best signal; costs a human-hour per robot-hour.
2. Simulation / synthetic data — unlimited, labelled; limited by the sim-to-real gap. NVIDIA reported generating 780 000 synthetic trajectories (≈6 500 hours) in 11 hours and a ~40 % gain for GR00T N1 when added to real data.
3. Human video (egocentric, web) — vast and diverse, but no action labels. Bridged by latent action models (LAPA: a VQ-VAE infers a discrete 'latent action' between frames; pre-train the policy on those, then swap in a real action head), hand-pose retargeting, or, as models scale, direct co-training.

Plus web image–text data inherited through the VLM backbone.
notes.source: NVIDIA newsroom, GR00T N1 announcement (GTC 2025) — https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-isaac-gr00t-n1-open-humanoid-robot-foundation-model-simulation-frameworks · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: How is reinforcement learning being applied to large VLA models?
notes.back:
Imitation alone plateaus below production-grade reliability and speed; RL lets the policy learn from its own experience.

• Fine-tune with task success as reward, often with human interventions/corrections mixed in (HIL-SERL-style).
• Advantage-conditioned training on autonomous roll-outs (Physical Intelligence's π*0.6 / RECAP) → large gains in throughput and failure rate on long real tasks.
• RL in the diffusion noise space (DSRL) or on a lightweight head/'RL token', leaving the big backbone frozen — avoids destabilising it.
• The other direction: a VLA issues high-level commands to a low-level RL locomotion/whole-body controller.
notes.source: Physical Intelligence research blog — https://www.pi.website/ · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: A VLA needs ~100 ms or more per inference, yet the robot must move smoothly at 50 Hz. How is that reconciled?
notes.back:
• Action chunking: one inference yields ~1 s of actions.
• Asynchronous inference: compute the next chunk while the current one executes.
• Real-Time Chunking (RTC): treat the actions that will already have been executed by the time inference finishes as frozen, and 'inpaint' the rest of the new chunk to be consistent with them (soft masking) → no pauses or jerks at chunk boundaries despite latency.
• Few-step flow matching, smaller System-1 networks, quantisation/TensorRT, token caching and early exit.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Why is evaluating generalist robot policies hard, and what benchmarks exist?
notes.back:
Real-world trials are slow, noisy, hardware- and lab-specific, and not reproducible; success rates depend on unreported details.

• Simulation: LIBERO (language-conditioned manipulation suites — now near-saturated), CALVIN (long-horizon), SimplerEnv (sim proxies of real set-ups), RoboCasa, ManiSkill, RoboTwin (bimanual).
• Real world: RoboArena — distributed, crowd-sourced pairwise comparisons of policies on the standardised DROID platform across many labs, aggregated into a ranking.

Treat vendor launch-day claims with caution; check live leaderboards and independent replications.
notes.source: Kawaharazuka et al. 2025, VLA Models for Robotics: A Review — https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07077 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: How can a hobbyist get hands-on with Physical AI for a few hundred euros?
notes.back:
Hugging Face LeRobot: open-source PyTorch library with datasets, tele-operation/recording tools and policy implementations (ACT, Diffusion Policy, π0, SmolVLA …).
SO-101: 3D-printable 6-DoF leader + follower arm pair driven by Feetech bus servos (~€100–250 in parts).

Workflow: tele-operate ~50 demonstrations with one or two cameras → dataset on the Hub → train ACT or fine-tune SmolVLA (~450M-parameter open VLA trained on community data, runs on a consumer GPU or laptop) → run the policy on the arm. The modern successor of the 'Arduino + servo arm' project.
notes.source: Hugging Face LeRobot — https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot · SmolVLA https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01844 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: Why are so many companies building humanoids, and what are the counter-arguments?
notes.back:
For: the world — stairs, doors, tools, workstations — is built for the human form, so one general body can take on many jobs; and human-shaped robots can exploit human data (tele-operation by retargeting, motion capture, egocentric video). Enablers: quasi-direct-drive actuators, sim-trained RL whole-body control, VLAs, on-board GPUs.
Against: legs add cost, energy use and fall risk where wheels suffice; dexterous hands and tactile sensing remain the bottleneck; reliability is far from industrial requirements (99.9 %+); safety certification around people is unresolved.

Players (2026): Figure, Tesla Optimus, 1X, Agility Digit, Apptronik Apollo, Boston Dynamics Atlas, Unitree G1/H1, AgiBot, UBTech.
notes.source: Figure AI, Helix 02 (Jan 2026) — https://www.figure.ai/news/helix-02 · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models

notes.deck: Robotics - Arduino to Physical AI::13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
notes.front: What safety layers does a learned robot policy still need?
notes.back:
A neural policy has no guarantees, so safety is enforced around it:
• Hardware/low level: emergency stop, torque/speed/workspace limits, collision detection, watchdogs and command time-outs — independent of the AI.
• Standards: ISO 10218 (industrial robots; revised 2025) and ISO/TS 15066 collaborative limits — power-and-force limiting, speed-and-separation monitoring; risk assessment per application.
• Control level: compliant/impedance control, control-barrier-function or MPC safety filters.
• Semantic safety: the model should reason about consequences (hot liquids, knives, people) — evaluated by benchmarks such as ASIMOV; plus human oversight, staged deployment and logging.
notes.source: ISO 10218-1/-2:2025 and ISO/TS 15066 — https://www.iso.org/ · 13 Physical AI & Robot Foundation Models
